```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(pdmS7)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  error = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 3.8, dpi = 120
)
pal <- c("#236b83", "#a26421", "#5b8c3a", "#8a3b6b", "#444444")
two_panels <- function() par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1), cex.main = 0.95)
```

PDM is a family of models, not one model. You choose a capacity distribution for the soil
store, a recharge rule that moves water to groundwater, and a routing form for each of the
surface and groundwater paths. This article shows how each choice behaves, so the choice can
rest on catchment behaviour rather than habit. [PDM explained](pdm-explained.html) gives the
equations; this article gives the consequences.

The default, `pdm_presets("standard")`, is the configuration Moore (2007) describes as most
widely used: a Pareto distribution, standard recharge, a two-store surface cascade and a cubic
groundwater store. Start there and change one component at a time.

| Component | Options | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Capacity distribution | Pareto, rectangular, exponential, triangular, lognormal | Pareto, b = 0.4 |
| Recharge | Standard, split, demand | Standard |
| Surface routing | Cascade of two linear stores, power-law store, exponential store | Cascade |
| Groundwater routing | Power-law store (linear, quadratic, cubic or any exponent), exponential store, cascade | Cubic |
| Groundwater solver | Adaptive Runge-Kutta, Smith approximation | Adaptive |

# The soil store: how fast does the catchment saturate?

The capacity distribution describes how storage capacity varies across the catchment. Its
shape decides how quickly the catchment starts producing runoff as it wets up. The five
families below all have a mean capacity of 100 mm, so they hold the same water when full; they
differ in how that capacity is spread.

```{r distributions, fig.cap="Left: the share of the catchment whose stores hold less than c. Right: direct runoff from one interval's net rainfall, with the soil store starting at 50 mm. The dotted line is runoff equal to rainfall."}
dists <- list(
  Pareto = FlodeParetoCapacity(0, 140, 0.4),
  Rectangular = FlodeRectangularCapacity(0, 200),
  Triangular = FlodeTriangularCapacity(0, 200),
  Exponential = FlodeExponentialCapacity(100),
  Lognormal = FlodeLognormalCapacity(log(100) - 0.5, 1)
)
cc <- seq(0, 300, length.out = 400)
net <- seq(0, 200, length.out = 200)
two_panels()
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 300), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Store capacity c (mm)",
     ylab = "Share of catchment below c", main = "Capacity distributions, mean 100 mm")
for (i in seq_along(dists)) {
  lines(cc, capacity_cdf(dists[[i]], cc), col = pal[i], lwd = 2, lty = i)
}
legend("bottomright", names(dists), col = pal, lty = 1:5, lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 200), ylim = c(0, 160), xlab = "Net rainfall in one interval (mm)",
     ylab = "Direct runoff (mm)", main = "Runoff from a storm, soil at 50 mm")
abline(0, 1, col = "grey70", lty = 3)
for (i in seq_along(dists)) {
  runoff <- vapply(net, function(p) soil_step(dists[[i]], 50, p)$runoff, numeric(1))
  lines(net, runoff, col = pal[i], lwd = 2, lty = i)
}
```

The bounded families (Pareto, rectangular, triangular) have a largest store, so a big enough
storm fills the catchment and every further millimetre runs off: the runoff line becomes
parallel to the dotted line. The unbounded families (exponential, lognormal) always keep some
deep stores unfilled, so they produce runoff earlier from small storms but never quite reach
full saturation.

## The Pareto shape parameter

Within the Pareto family, the exponent `b` is usually the most informative parameter to
calibrate. With `b = 0` every store has the same capacity, so nothing runs off until the whole
catchment is full. Larger values add more shallow stores, which produce runoff early.

```{r pareto-b, fig.cap="Pareto distributions with cmax = 200 mm. Right: runoff with the soil store starting at 40 per cent of its capacity."}
bs <- c(0, 0.2, 0.4, 1, 2)
two_panels()
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 200), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Store capacity c (mm)", ylab = "F(c)",
     main = "Pareto, cmax = 200 mm")
for (i in seq_along(bs)) {
  lines(cc[cc <= 200], capacity_cdf(FlodeParetoCapacity(0, 200, bs[i]), cc[cc <= 200]),
        col = pal[i], lwd = 2, lty = i)
}
legend("topleft", paste("b =", bs), col = pal, lty = 1:5, lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 200), ylim = c(0, 160), xlab = "Net rainfall (mm)",
     ylab = "Direct runoff (mm)", main = "Runoff, soil at 40 per cent of capacity")
for (i in seq_along(bs)) {
  d <- FlodeParetoCapacity(0, 200, bs[i])
  start <- 0.4 * capacity_mean(d)
  runoff <- vapply(net, function(p) soil_step(d, start, p)$runoff, numeric(1))
  lines(net, runoff, col = pal[i], lwd = 2, lty = i)
}
```

A rule of thumb: flashy, thin-soiled catchments suit larger `b`; permeable catchments that
absorb small storms suit smaller `b`. Calibration should decide, but the plot shows why `b`
and `cmax` trade off against each other.

# Recharge: how water reaches groundwater

The three recharge rules produce very different baseflow from the same storms. The models
below differ only in recharge, and each starts in steady state with the same observed flow
(see [Starting a run](starting-states.html)), so the comparison is fair from the first hour.

```{r recharge, fig.cap="Two storms over 25 days, hourly steps. Left: total flow. Right: the baseflow component alone."}
n <- 24 * 25
rain <- rep(0, n)
rain[24 * 2 + 1:12] <- 4
rain[24 * 9 + 1:6] <- 8
forcing <- data.frame(rain = rain, pet = 0.05)
days <- seq_len(n) / 24
recharge <- list(
  Standard = FlodeStandardRecharge(kg = 200, bg = 1, st = 0),
  Split = FlodeSplitRecharge(alpha = 0.6),
  Demand = FlodeDemandRecharge(alpha = 0.5, beta = 1.5, qsat = 0.4)
)
runs <- lapply(recharge, function(r) {
  model <- pdm_model(recharge = r, groundwater = cubic_routing(kb = 2000), area_km2 = 50)
  state <- initial_state_from_flow(model, observed_m3s = 1, baseflow_fraction = 0.7,
                                   soil_fraction = 0.6)
  run_pdm(model, forcing, state)$output
})
two_panels()
plot(NA, xlim = range(days), ylim = c(0, max(sapply(runs, function(o) max(o$q_m3s)))),
     xlab = "Day", ylab = "Flow (m3/s)", main = "Total flow")
for (i in seq_along(runs)) lines(days, runs[[i]]$q_m3s, col = pal[i], lwd = 2, lty = i)
legend("topright", names(runs), col = pal, lty = 1:3, lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
baseflow <- lapply(runs, function(o) o$baseflow_out_mm * 50 / 3.6)
plot(NA, xlim = range(days), ylim = c(0, max(unlist(baseflow))), xlab = "Day",
     ylab = "Baseflow (m3/s)", main = "Baseflow component")
for (i in seq_along(runs)) lines(days, baseflow[[i]], col = pal[i], lwd = 2, lty = i)
```

- **Standard** recharge drains the soil store in proportion to its storage above a tension
  threshold. It gives smooth, sustained baseflow: the usual choice.
- **Split** recharge sends a fixed share of direct runoff to groundwater and nothing from the
  soil store itself. Baseflow rises and falls with each storm, so recessions are short. It
  suits catchments with little groundwater.
- **Demand** recharge depends on how much the groundwater store can take. When groundwater is
  low the soil drains fast, at up to `qsat`, which gives the plateau; once groundwater fills,
  recharge falls back. Its behaviour depends strongly on the time step, so check results at
  more than one step before relying on it.

# Routing: the shape of the recession

Each routing store turns its inflow into outflow through a storage-discharge relationship.
The relationship sets the shape of the recession once rain stops.

```{r routing, fig.cap="Left: recessions from an outflow of 1 mm/h with no further inflow, on a log scale. Right: the storage needed for each outflow, scaled so that storage at 1 mm/h is 1."}
routes <- list(
  Linear = linear_routing(48), Quadratic = quadratic_routing(2000),
  Cubic = cubic_routing(20000), Exponential = FlodeExponentialRouting(0.05, -2)
)
hours <- 0:(24 * 20)
two_panels()
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 20), ylim = c(0.01, 1), log = "y", xlab = "Day",
     ylab = "Outflow (mm/h, log scale)", main = "Recession with no inflow")
for (i in seq_along(routes)) {
  r <- routes[[i]]
  storage <- storage_for_flow(r, 1)
  q <- numeric(length(hours))
  q[1] <- 1
  for (h in 2:length(hours)) {
    step <- route_step(r, storage, 0, 1)
    storage <- step$storage
    q[h] <- step$q_end
  }
  lines(hours / 24, q, col = pal[i], lwd = 2, lty = i)
}
legend("bottomleft", names(routes), col = pal, lty = 1:4, lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
qq <- seq(0.001, 1, length.out = 200)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Outflow q (mm/h)",
     ylab = "Relative storage", main = "Storage needed for each outflow")
for (i in seq_along(routes)) {
  r <- routes[[i]]
  low <- storage_for_flow(r, 0.001)
  high <- storage_for_flow(r, 1)
  lines(qq, (storage_for_flow(r, qq) - low) / (high - low), col = pal[i], lwd = 2, lty = i)
}
```

A linear store recedes exponentially, which is a straight line on the log scale. Nonlinear
stores recede fast at high flow and slowly at low flow, which matches most observed
baseflow: that is why Moore recommends the cubic store for groundwater. The exponential store
has the longest tail of the four, for catchments whose baseflow persists through long dry
spells.

The surface path normally uses the cascade of two linear stores, which shapes the storm
hydrograph's rise and fall with two time constants, `k1` and `k2`. Either path can use any of
the routing forms.

# Groundwater solver: adaptive or Smith

The cubic store can be solved two ways. The adaptive solver integrates the store equation to
a tight tolerance. The Smith solver uses a closed-form approximation from Moore (2007), Eq. 24,
which is slightly faster but loses accuracy as the time step grows.

```{r solver, fig.cap="Largest flow error of the Smith solver, as a percentage of peak flow, against the time step. Errors are measured against the adaptive solver with a very tight tolerance, on 60 days of synthetic forcing."}
set.seed(1)
n15 <- 96 * 60
rain15 <- ifelse(stats::runif(n15) < 0.08, stats::rgamma(n15, 0.7, scale = 1), 0)
steps <- c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 6, 12, 24)
aggregate_steps <- function(x, k) colSums(matrix(x[seq_len(floor(length(x) / k) * k)], k))
smith_error <- function(kb) {
  vapply(steps, function(dt) {
    k <- dt / 0.25
    f <- data.frame(rain = aggregate_steps(rain15, k), pet = 0.02 * k)
    build <- function(solver, rtol = 1e-8) {
      suppressWarnings(pdm_model(area_km2 = 50, dt = dt, groundwater = power_routing(
        k = 1 / kb, m = 3, solver = solver, rtol = rtol, atol = 1e-12
      )))
    }
    ref <- run_pdm(build("adaptive", 1e-12), f)$output$q_m3s
    smith <- run_pdm(build("smith"), f)$output$q_m3s
    100 * max(abs(smith - ref)) / max(ref)
  }, numeric(1))
}
kbs <- c(1000, 10000, 50000)
errors <- sapply(kbs, smith_error)
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
matplot(steps, errors, type = "b", log = "xy", pch = 16, lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = pal[1:3],
        xlab = "Time step (hours, log scale)", ylab = "Smith error, % of peak (log scale)",
        yaxt = "n")
axis(2, at = c(0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100), labels = c("0.01", "0.1", "1", "10", "100"), las = 1)
abline(v = 1, lty = 3, col = "grey50")
legend("topleft", paste("kb =", format(kbs, big.mark = ",")), col = pal[1:3], lwd = 2,
       pch = 16, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

The error grows roughly with the square of the step. Up to a 1-hour step it stays near or
below 1 per cent of peak flow, so `pdm_model()` warns once per session if Smith is used with a
longer step. Use the adaptive solver, the default, unless you need the last quarter of speed
at a 15-minute step.

# Snow

In catchments where snow matters, the PACK snowpack runs before PDM and passes on the rain
and melt that leave the pack. See [PACK snowpack explained](snowpack-explained.html).

## Source

Moore, R. J. (2007). The PDM rainfall-runoff model. *Hydrology and Earth System Sciences*
11, 483-499. https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-11-483-2007
